transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-16
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Meyer (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Citrine - Platform Eng), Maya Rivera (Citrine - AI Lead), Jon Park (Citrine - SRE)

Summary:
Quick demo focused on: long-context handling when TPS spikes, how streaming backpressure surfaces in the Redwood runtime, what telemetry to look at in Console + Optimize recommendations to avoid timeouts. Customer provided a scenario where they ingest docs with 250k token context, and at the same time have bursty 150-250 TPS. Goal: see graceful degradation patterns and configuration levers.

Topics:
- Long-context KV cache behavior and eviction
- Streaming backpressure and client-side read timeouts
- Autoscaling and burst windows on Dedicated
- Telemetry signals to detect queueing and per-request tail latency
- Fallback policies: smaller quantized variant vs model-level shedding

Action items (in-meeting recap): Jordan to share pilot pricing; Priya to run a guided console walkthrough; Ethan to provide traces.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll try to keep this to an hour but Priya and I have a couple of demos lined up. Is the agenda ok?
[00:08] Ethan: Yep, thanks, Jordan. We're mostly interested in two things — how you handle these huge contexts and what happens when our TPS spikes, like say from 40 to 220 requests per second in a 10 minute window, and our front-end can't wait forever.
[00:20] Maya: Also curious about observability — how quickly do you see the queue forming, and can we tie that back to cost?
[00:27] Priya: Cool, great — quick note: some of the terminology might get a little fuzzy in the transcript — SE sometimes shows up as Speaker 2, so apologies if names look off.
[00:35] Jordan: I'll hand off to Priya to show the Console. Priya?
[00:38] Priya: Thanks. I'm going to share my screen — first thing: Console telemetry. Here you can see per-model token throughput, tail latency P95/P99 and a queue depth metric. For this demo I have a synthetic workload: a long-context generator that creates 200-300k token sessions with repeating prefixes so kv cache is exercised.
[01:05] Priya: Right now baseline is 20 TPS, then at 05:00 into the run I blow it up to 220 TPS for 7 minutes to emulate your burst. Watch the queue depth and the stream commit latency.
[01:16] Jon: When you say stream commit, do you mean the latency between chunk sends over HTTP/2 / SSE? That's the point our clients hit timeouts.
[01:23] Priya: Correct. There are two observable latencies: server processing token latency, and network/stream commit latency. When queueing occurs, token latency stays relatively stable for cached prefixes, but commit latency climbs because selected kernel time increases and batching windows widen.
[01:38] [01:38] (screen noise)
[01:42] Priya: Alright I triggered the spike — watch P99 - it climbs from 430ms to ~2.8s during the peak. Queue depth goes from 3 to 42. You can also see a KV cache eviction rate tick up — that's the key signal for long context sessions.
[02:00] Maya: Is the KV cache eviction you show global or per-session? We saw some mem blow-up in our PoC and want to understand lifecycle.
[02:08] Priya: It's per-worker. Each GPU worker tracks a session-level KV footprint; the console aggregates evictions per model instance. We offer TTLs and eviction policies — LRU-ish — and you can pin prefixes for critical flows. Note: pinning costs memory so there is a tradeoff.
[02:27] Ethan: If the cache evicts mid-session, do you stream a message to the client indicating partial context loss? Our client would like to gracefully fallback.
[02:35] Priya: We emit trace events and a metadata field in the streaming frames that indicates cache miss / re-requested history. There's no automatic restatement of the prompt — that's application-level logic normally. But we do provide a model-variant fallback: switch to a quantized variant that has smaller KV footprint under severe memory pressure. That reduces quality slightly but keeps latency bounded.
[02:56] Jordan: Can you show what happens when a client-side read timeout occurs during the spike?
[03:00] Priya: Sure — I'm going to flip to the trace view.
[03:05] Priya: Here is a sample request. You can see the timeline: request arrived, enqueued, started execution, tokens produced and then a client read timeout at 9.4 seconds. The server continued generation for a little bit, then the runtime detected the socket close and aborted; we have a graceful abort path so GPU resources are freed immediately.
[03:28] Jon: So we shouldn't see zombie GPU ops? That's been our main worry.
[03:32] Priya: Correct — we have a cancellation propagation that tears down the KV session and frees the cache slots promptly. There's a short bleed window (~100-200ms) for cleanup.
[03:41] Ethan: What about batching? If we have 200 TPS, does Redwood batch across requests and increase latency for everyone?
[03:47] Priya: Continuous batching is workload-aware. For high concurrency the runtime shortens the batching window to keep latency under SLO; we also have policy attributes on a per-route basis. So you can set max_batch_delay or prioritized routes for low-latency traffic. For your use case we'd recommend a two-tier route: interactive (low delay, smaller batch) and bulk (higher throughput, larger batch).
[04:10] Maya: Do you show effective per-token cost under those two tiers? We want to model economics.
[04:15] Priya: Yes — Console shows tokens per second and cost estimate per minute under a cost model. When you enable KV pinning you'll see an increase in GPU memory usage and cost; Optimize will give suggestions like quantize to int8 and reduce sequence length sample windows.
[04:28] Jordan: Quick interjection — some words get munged in auto-transcripts — for example, we sometimes see 'KV cache' as 'K-V cash', or 'tokenizer' as 'token laser' in older exports.
[04:38] (laughter)
[04:40] Ethan: Happy to hear that. Priya, can you trigger a fallback to the quantized model now so we can see quality delta and latency?
[04:46] Priya: Yep. I'm switching routing policy to prefer the quantized variant when worker memory > 86%. Watch P50/P95.
[04:55] Priya: Switching now — there is a short model swap; P95 drops from 1.2s to 760ms, and model perplexity on the test prompt rises slightly — you'll see minor token variances in the transcript but overall coherence stays acceptable for QA tasks.
[05:12] Maya: Slightly worried about hallucinations. Do you have quality regression alerts?
[05:17] Priya: Optimize includes a regression monitor. You can attach a prompt-suite; if rouge/embedding divergence crosses a threshold after a rollout it will trigger an alert and optionally rollback the route.
[05:29] Jon: Backpressure — can we get push notifications when queue depth or evictions cross thresholds? We have an incident playbook we want to integrate.
[05:36] Priya: Yes, Console supports webhooks and pager integrations. There are also event streams you can subscribe to for queue depth, active sessions, evictions per minute.
[05:45] [05:45] (background typing)
[05:50] Priya: I'm going to show the live log of the runtime, there are a few interesting fields. One is kvcache_size_bytes, another is active_sessions, then queue_ms which is the metric you want to watch. When queue_ms > 5000 we start invoking fallback policies — by default that is model-variant fallback, then region fallback if enabled.
[06:12] Ethan: Region fallback is attractive for resilience, but it could have residency implications for us — some of our data must remain in-region.
[06:19] Priya: Understood — Dedicated and Private modes allow you to restrict region fallback. We'll never automatically move data cross-region for private deployments without your policy.
[06:29] Jordan: Can we do a quick deep-dive on request-level timeouts? Maya, what's your client default?
[06:34] Maya: Browser-side we have a 10s read timeout for the streaming channel, mobile is 12s.
[06:40] Priya: Ok that helps. For 10s timeouts you should set client keepalive pings and chunked chunk sizes so the stream sends small tokens early. Also consider preemptive partial summaries: if you know the user is likely to request long-context answers, the client can ask for a summarized history to reduce tokens before the heavy generate.
[06:58] Jon: How do keepalive pings affect throughput? Are they counted as requests?
[07:02] Priya: They are lightweight heartbeat frames; they don't use model tokens but do consume network and concurrent session slots. In high TPS regimes heartbeats may add overhead, so tune ping frequency.
[07:12] Priya: I'm going to run a synthetic where I reduce chunk size from 4k tokens to 512 tokens per payload to emulate early flush.
[07:20] [07:20] (demo running)
[07:25] Priya: With smaller chunks P99 drops by ~600ms because clients receive meaningful data earlier and are less likely to timeout. Downside: parceling increases per-request overhead slightly and can raise token billing for meta tokens if you restructure prompts.
[07:42] Maya: Hmm — that seems promising. For our render flow we can start with smaller primitives.
[07:48] Ethan: Can Redwood instrument the SDK to suggest chunk sizes automatically?
[07:52] Priya: We have an SDK mode 'adaptive_chunking' in beta that watches client read latencies and adjusts chunk size per session. We'll include that in the pilot if you want.
[08:03] Jordan: We'll note that as an action item.
[08:06] Priya: Now I'm going to simulate client read timeouts during a long-running generation so you can see a full lifecycle with cancellation and memory reclamation.
[08:16] [08:16] (synthetic spike)
[08:20] Priya: Timeout at 9.8s, cancellation routed, kvcache freed, active_sessions down by one. There's also an alert we can show in the console.
[08:30] Jon: Great. I want to dig into autoscaling — if we autoscale workers to absorb bursts how long is cold spin-up?
[08:37] Priya: For Dedicated we offer warm pools which keep N workers hot. Cold spin-up on bare GPU instances can be 60-90s depending on image. Warm pools shave that to <6s for model warmstart when the model already has a compiled kernel cache. There's also a burst window feature where you can temporarily exceed committed capacity for short intervals.
[09:00] Ethan: What's the cost model for warm pools and burst windows? Do we pay base + burst?
[09:06] Priya: Yes — warm pools have a standby fee lower than active GPU time. Burst windows are billed at a premium per GPU-hour for the burst duration. We'll include detailed numbers in the pricing doc.
[09:18] Maya: On the security side — we need SOC2 Type II, SSO, and KMS integration. Are these supported in the pilot?
[09:25] Jordan: Yes — we support SAML SSO and KMS integration for Dedicated and Private. We'll attach SOC2 docs to the follow-up email.
[09:34] Ethan: For the benchmark run we want two scenarios: 1) long-context heavy (200-300k token sessions) at 30 TPS baseline + 220 TPS burst, and 2) batch summarization jobs (no streaming) with 500 concurrent jobs.
[09:47] Priya: We'll provision a dedicated pool and run both. For the first scenario we'll enable kv pinning for a subset to see effect.
[09:55] [09:55] (murmurs)
[10:00] Priya: I'm going to show the Optimize recommendations — here the system suggests: reduce max-history-window from 3e5 to 1.2e5 tokens for mixed workloads, enable int8 quant, and set route priority for interactive flows. It also gives projected cost delta and latency improvement.
[10:20] Maya: Can Optimize suggest a per-route policy automatically from our traffic trace?
[10:25] Priya: Yes — if you upload the 48hr trace, Optimize will evaluate traffic distribution and propose route configs with estimated cost/latency tradeoffs. It uses a simulation layer to estimate queuing.
[10:36] Ethan: We use on-prem K8s — how invasive is the Private deployment? We cannot have outbound control planes for data.
[10:43] Priya: Private has an optional air-gapped package. Control plane can be run in your VPC, and there is an on-prem runtime with KMS integration. It does require some infra work but our solutions team handles the kick-off.
[10:58] Jordan: Quick note — occasionally our transcripts render Kubernetes as 'Q-Bernettes' in the raw file — it's an amusing artifact.
[11:06] (laughter)
[11:09] Ethan: Ok, next I want to raise an edge-case: what if we have a long context user session that starts as interactive, then someone kicks off a heavy background summarization from the same session ID — do you isolate those operations?
[11:23] Priya: We recommend splitting interactive and background into separate routes. The runtime does session affinity by default but you can tag requests with a request-type header so the router puts them into different queues and enforces per-route concurrency caps.
[11:36] Jon: If an interactive session is pinned to a worker and a background job hogs memory, can it evict pinned prefixes?
[11:44] Priya: Pinned prefixes are last-resort, but under absolute OOM we may evict—they are best effort. For strict isolation use Dedicated pools with memory reservations.
[11:57] Maya: Could you demo a regression alert firing if quantized model quality degrades?
[12:02] Priya: Sure. I'm going to do a canary rollout and push 10% of traffic. The monitoring detects a spike in embedding divergence above threshold and auto-rolls back the canary. See the alert and the rollback action.
[12:20] Ethan: Nice. Does the rollback cause any warm-start coldness for the primary model?
[12:25] Priya: We roll back at the router level; the primary remains hot. There is no significant cold penalty if both variants were previously warmed.
[12:33] Jordan: We're nearing the end — any final questions?
[12:36] Jon: A last one — how are session logs kept and what's retention? We need 90-day logs for SRE.
[12:42] Priya: Console allows configurable log retention per account; default is 30 days, enterprise can go to 365. You can also stream logs to your SIEM or S3 for longer retention.
[12:53] Maya: Ok great — next steps as you outlined. We'll send the traces and propose benchmark dates.
[13:00] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the SOC2 and pricing and schedule the pilot.
